Health and behaviour

How stress, habits and beliefs influence physical health, and how behaviours are changed.

Level 1 · Short introduction

Many of the leading causes of illness and death are related to behaviour: smoking, diet, inactivity, alcohol and whether or not a treatment is followed. Health psychology studies how stress, emotions, beliefs and the environment influence physical health, and how to help people change habits. It is a field where family medicine and psychology work very closely.

Level 2 · Fuller explanation

Stress

In 1936 Hans Selye described the body's general response to prolonged threats. In 1984 Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman added that stress depends on how we appraise the situation and our resources to cope. Brief stress is useful; chronic stress is associated with worse cardiovascular health, worse sleep and an altered immune response.

Changing behaviour

  • Motivational interviewing (William Miller and Stephen Rollnick): a conversational style that helps people explore their own ambivalence instead of trying to convince them. It is well supported for alcohol use and other behaviours.
  • Implementation intentions (Peter Gollwitzer): concrete "if X happens, I will do Y" plans increase the likelihood of doing what we set out to do.
  • Environment: changing what is within reach, such as putting fruit in view, often works better than appealing to willpower.

Adherence

According to the WHO, in chronic illnesses about half of patients do not follow treatment as prescribed. There are many reasons: side effects, forgetting, doubts about usefulness, cost or poor communication with the professional. Asking without judging and simplifying regimens helps.

Quitting smoking

Tobacco is the leading preventable cause of death. Quitting is hard because of nicotine dependence and associated habits. Combining psychological support with medication clearly raises the chances of success: between 70% higher and double compared with brief advice, according to a Cochrane review. Most people need several attempts, and each attempt teaches something.

Communicating with patients

A good relationship between professional and patient improves adherence and outcomes. Asking what the person knows and fears, explaining in plain words and checking understanding ("can you tell me how you'll take it?") are simple techniques with evidence behind them.

Level 3 · Going further, with references

Adverse childhood experiences

The ACE study by Vincent Felitti and Robert Anda (1998), with over 17,000 adults in California, found that the more adverse childhood experiences a person had had (abuse, neglect, violence at home, addiction or mental illness in the family), the greater their risk of heart and lung disease, depression and substance use in adulthood. It is a population-level association: it cannot predict any one person's future, and many people with adverse experiences enjoy good health.

Pain

Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall's gate control theory of pain (1965) showed that pain is not a simple damage signal: the brain modulates it according to attention, emotions and expectations. Today chronic pain treatments combine exercise, pain education and psychological therapies.

Placebo and nocebo

Expectations can relieve symptoms (placebo) and also produce them (nocebo). In statin trials, many of the muscle pains attributed to the drug also appeared with placebo, according to a 2021 study in which patients unknowingly alternated between real pills, placebo and months without treatment.

Medically unexplained symptoms

In primary care many consultations are due to persistent physical symptoms without a clear organic cause, such as pain, fatigue or dizziness. They are real and cause suffering. The approach that works best combines carefully ruling out serious causes, explaining the mechanisms of the body and stress, avoiding unnecessary tests and agreeing a gradual activity plan.
